paragraphs: Seven fostering services list Croydon as an area they cover, all of them independent agencies, and they are shown above. The council also runs its own service, Foster Croydon. Fostering for the council means caring for Croydon's own children with the council's social workers behind you; an independent agency assesses, trains and supervises its carers itself, and councils, Croydon included, ask agencies to find homes when they cannot place a child with their own carers.

Croydon relies on both. Its market position statement for 2025 to 2027 says that in June 2025, 189 of the borough's fostered children (45%) lived with carers from independent agencies and the other 227 (55%) with other foster carers, and it names carers who live in Croydon itself among the people it most needs.

The fostering service's annual report for 2025-26 shows interest rising. It had 152 approved fostering households on 31 March 2026, up from 139 a year earlier, and received 1,079 requests for information against a target of 300. Eleven households were approved against a target of 15, with ten more still in assessment at the year end. The report says Croydon wants more choice for adolescents, large groups of brothers and sisters, unaccompanied minors and young people at risk of exploitation, and for some disabled children with specialist needs. It has introduced skilled, advanced and specialist fostering pathways and plans to develop care for emergencies.

Support is local too. Croydon has launched three Horizons Hubs, each led by an experienced foster carer, where carers, their own children and the young people they look after can connect and support one another, with planned sleepovers for a break and help in a crisis. The hubs build on a pilot that brought six foster families together.

The council raised carer payments by up to 30%, the first change since rates were last reviewed in 2022, and calls itself one of the most competitive and supportive councils in the south of England. Our Croydon allowance page sets out the scale: a weekly allowance for each child from £208 for under-fives to £309 for 16 and 17-year-olds, plus a weekly skills fee of £325 at entry level, £450 at the advanced level and £600 for specialist roles, so a newly approved carer receives £533 to £634 a week for one child. Carers also get Council Tax reimbursement and a £1,500 retention bonus each year after three years with Croydon, and carers who transfer receive a £1,500 welcome payment. Talk to the council and two or three of the agencies above before you choose, and see the Bromley, Sutton, Merton and Lambeth pages, or London as a whole, if you live near the borough's edge.
